![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14119247/assets/4807f92defb4202359a32ca046073cd138db396a0975164e42b96126ac0cc591.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)={e}^{x}\,i+{e}^{-2y}\,j$ and $C$ is the arc of a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin traversed counterclockwise from the point $(1,0)$ to the point $(0,1)?$

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.$*
question.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize a part-circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin. This curve can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & ={e}^{x}\,i+{e}^{-2y}\,j \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,i+{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,i+{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$
